title: Net Positions by Symbol

statement.md: At the end of a trading day, a desk's blotter holds a long list of executed trades: buys (positive quantity) and sells (negative quantity) in many symbols. Before anything else — risk, settlement, reporting — the blotter is *netted*: all trades in the same symbol collapse to a single signed net position. This is a textbook streaming hash-table aggregation, and getting it right (including output order and 64-bit accumulation) is a daily engineering task on any trading floor.

Read n trade lines, each containing a symbol and a signed integer quantity. Accumulate the net quantity per symbol and print one line per distinct symbol, sorted by symbol in ascending lexicographic (byte-wise) order, as SYMBOL followed by a space and the net quantity. Symbols that net to exactly 0 are still printed.

statement.title: Sorting detail
statement.md: Symbols consist of uppercase letters A-Z and digits 0-9. Byte-wise order puts digits before letters (0 < 9 < A < Z) and shorter prefixes first (A10 < B1 < B2). This is exactly the order produced by sorting the strings as byte strings / lexicographically, which is what Python's sorted() and C++ std::map both do for such inputs.

inputFormat: Line 1: the integer n. Each of the next n lines contains a token SYM (1 to 10 characters, each A-Z or 0-9) and an integer qty (-10^9 <= qty <= 10^9), separated by a space.
outputFormat: One line per distinct symbol, in ascending lexicographic order of the symbol: SYM NET where NET is the signed sum of all quantities for that symbol.
constraints: The absolute net per symbol fits in a signed 64-bit integer (it is at most 2*10^14). Accumulate in 64-bit; 32-bit will overflow.

6
AAPL 100
MSFT -50
AAPL -30
TSLA 25
MSFT -20

examples.explanation: AAPL: 100 - 30 + 5 = 75. MSFT: -50 - 20 = -70. TSLA: 25. Sorted: AAPL, MSFT, TSLA.
AAPL nets to exactly 0 and is still printed. Alphabetical order: AAA, AAPL, ZZZ.

hints: One pass: hash map from symbol to running net, adding each signed quantity as you read it.
Sort the distinct symbols once at the end and print each with its net. In C++ a std::map<string,long long> keeps keys sorted for free.
Net positions easily exceed 32-bit range: 2*10^5 trades of +/-10^9 reach 2*10^14. Use long long / Python ints.

editorial.md: This is the canonical aggregate-by-key pattern. A hash map (dictionary) maps each symbol to its running net: for each trade, net[sym] += qty, an expected O(1) update. After the single pass, extract the keys, sort them (O(s log s) for s distinct symbols), and print. Total: $O(n + s \log s)$ time, $O(s)$ memory — a single scan over the tape and no per-trade sorting.

editorial.title: Worked example
items: Trades: AAPL +100, MSFT -50, AAPL -30, TSLA +25, MSFT -20, AAPL +5.
Sorted symbols: AAPL, MSFT, TSLA. Output AAPL 75 / MSFT -70 / TSLA 25.

editorial.md: Two details deserve care. First, zero-net symbols must still appear: netting is an accounting identity, not a filter. Second, accumulation must be 64-bit — with quantity bounds of 10^9 and up to 2*10^5 trades, a 32-bit accumulator overflows long before the end of the tape. In C++ prefer std::map<string,long long> (sorted automatically) or unordered_map plus an explicit sort of keys; both are acceptable here.

editorial.title: Netting in practice
editorial.md: Real post-trade systems net fills per account per symbol per settlement date, then compare against expected positions. The same hash-accumulate-report shape powers VWAP buckets, PnL aggregation, and exchange drop-copy reconciliation — it is arguably the most-executed loop in a trading back office.

solutions.python:
import sys

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
    n = int(data[0])
    net = {}
    idx = 1
    for _ in range(n):
        sym = data[idx].decode(); q = int(data[idx + 1]); idx += 2
        net[sym] = net.get(sym, 0) + q
    out = []
    for sym in sorted(net):
        out.append(f"{sym} {net[sym]}")
    sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out) + "\n")

main()
